<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<span class="ltx_personname">M.Reza Ebrahimi

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the remarkable practical success of transformer-based language models, recent work has raised concerns about their ability to perform state tracking. In particular, a growing body of literature has shown this limitation primarily through failures in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, such as length extrapolation. In this work, we shift attention to the in-distribution implications of these limitations. We conduct a large-scale experimental study of the data efficiency of transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) across multiple supervision regimes. We find that the amount of training data required by transformers grows much more rapidly with state-space size and sequence length than for RNNs. Furthermore, we analyze the extent to which learned state-tracking mechanisms are shared across different sequence lengths. We show that transformers exhibit negligible or even detrimental weight sharing across lengths, indicating that they learn length-specific solutions in isolation. In contrast, recurrent models exhibit effective amortized learning by sharing weights across lengths, allowing data from one sequence length to improve performance on others. Together, these results demonstrate that state tracking remains a fundamental challenge for transformers, even when training and evaluation distributions match.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">State tracking is a key capability of most intelligent systems and of
most models of computation. It is the process of monitoring and updating
the status of an entity or process with which the system interacts over
a period of time. State tracking is particularly important in
multi-hop, interactive tasks, such as that of an agent interacting with
an interface or of a dialogue system interacting with a user across
multiple turns.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">State tracking has become a popular area of investigation in recent
years, especially in the study of LLM capabilities and failure modes.
In this context, numerous studies have shown that transformer-based
models are fundamentally limited in their ability to perform
state tracking (for example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anil et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dziri et al., 2024</a>)</cite>).
This contrasts with recurrent networks, which excel at state tracking
(although their wide-spread applicability is unfortunately hampered by their relative
training inefficiency).
The limitations of transformers have been
demonstrated as limitations in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization,
specifically length-generalization: after training models on tasks encoded
in sequences of a given range of lengths, they were evaluated on sequences
with lengths that were not seen during training.
In these scenarios, the trained models fail to consistently generate correct
outputs on the evaluation data, although they are able to solve the tasks for
even unseen sequences in the training range of lengths.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">It could be argued that in any real-world use cases, OOD state tracking failures
may not be an issue as long as enough training data with step-by-step sequential
supervision is available. If training data covers all sequence lengths
that may be encountered at inference time, inference can rely entirely
on in-distribution generalization.
Unfortunately, although this argument is true in principle,
it is hard to quantify “enough” in this context. It is also hard
to quantify how the amount of training data required for any given task may depend
on the length of the sequences and the size of the state space.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To shed light on these questions, in this work we perform a detailed and systematic
empirical study of the <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">in-distribution</em> performance of transformer-based
models and contrast these with recurrent models. To this end, we train
and evaluate a range of representative models on a range of simple
state tracking tasks.
Independently varying sequence length and size of
the state space in these tasks then allows us to discover regularities in
the dependence of generalization error on these parameters.
This in turn makes it possible to obtain a crude “lower bound” of the minimal amount
of training data likely required to solve such tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A key difference between transformer-based and recurrent models is that,
at every timestep, the former compute outputs by applying a function
that depends on <em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">all</em> inputs and outputs generated previously (the context window),
making it possible, in principle, to re-calculate the required state from the past
information globally at each time step.
Recurrent networks, on the other hand, compute outputs by applying a function that
depends on only the current hidden state, making it impossible to perform such a re-calculation.
This makes it strictly necessary for a recurrent network to encode any relevant information
from the past within a single hidden state vector.
This inductive bias encourages a recurrent network to
incorporate the information from the current
timestep into its representation of state at the moment where this
information is available. Conversely, it discourages it from “saving”
this information off to determine future state updates globally from
the past information. The immediate state updates thus encourage the
network to process the input sequence step-by-step,
making any state update explicit as soon as this is possible,
rather than potentially deferring such updates to a later point in time.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Such step-by-step state updates are a natural inductive bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mitchell, 1997</a>)</cite>
in the context of simple state tracking tasks, as they make it possible to reduce complex
multi-step dependencies to a sequence of single-step computations.
They also allow a model to share weights across multiple different
sequence lengths, as it breaks state updates into single-step,
repeatable computations.
By analogy to the induction step in a mathematical proof,
we shall refer to this kind of inductive bias in this work
as “induction bias” (sic).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, the presence of the induction bias in a model means
that the joint distribution over tokens, conditioned on
the most recent hidden state, factorizes, such that
<math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(x_{t+1}|x_{1},\ldots,x_{t},h_{t})=p(x_{t+1}|x_{t},h_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(x_{t+1}|x_{1},\ldots,x_{t},h_{t})=p(x_{t+1}|x_{t},h_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> is the <math id="S1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math><sup id="S1.p7.1.1" class="ltx_sup">th</sup> token and <math id="S1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>
the hidden state in timestep <math id="S1.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, representing a <em id="S1.p7.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">minimal
sufficient statistic</em> for determining <math id="S1.p7.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the presence (or respectively absence) of an
induction bias, or its relative strength, provides a simple
explanation for a wide range of the empirical findings we present.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p9.1" class="ltx_p">Key take-aways from our study include the following:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that there is a distinct difference between the supervision regimes
in which transformers and recurrent networks perform well in-distribution.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that transformers can relatively efficiently learn state tracking
tasks in-distribution on one (fixed) sequence length at a time, but generalizing in-distribution
over multiple sequence lengths requires significantly more training data.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present evidence that, unlike recurrent networks,
transformers tend to fail at sharing parameters across sequence lengths and instead learn separate solution mechanisms for different lengths.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show that the degree of knowledge transfer across multiple different sequence
lengths in the in-distribution setting is highly correlated with the ability of a model to length-generalize.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">1.1 </span>Related work</h3>

<div id="S1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A range of studies has shown that transformer-based sequence models fail to length-generalize
in state tracking tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anil et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deletang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dziri et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abbe et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Unlike our work, these studies solely discuss OOD scenarios, while we discuss in-distribution data efficiency instead.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The inability to length-generalize in state tracking tasks has been shown to hold also for
most existing state-space models (SSM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sarrof et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cirone et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shakerinava et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
However recent work has shown that
making the hidden-to-hidden transition matrix in the SSM input-dependent and non-diagonal
can recover the ability to length-generalize.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grazzi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi and Memisevic, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Terzić et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Terzić et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al. (2025)</a></cite> show that transformers solve state tracking tasks in-distribution
by making use of parallel mechanisms reminiscent of associative scan. While this view can help
explain the OOD failures of these models, it also hints at the absence of an “induction” bias
which affects data efficiency as we show in this work.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Methodology</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task:</span> 
We consider the task of modular addition, where a model is provided a sequence of <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> integers <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> with each <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> drawn uniformly at random from <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{Z}_{m}=\{0,1,\dots,m-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{Z}_{m}=\{0,1,\dots,m-1\}</annotation></semantics></math>. The objective is to compute the sum of the sequence modulo <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)\!\!\!\!\!\!\pmod{m},\quad x_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{m}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mpadded style="width:0em;" width="0em"><mo>)</mo></mpadded></mrow><mspace style="width:0.949em;" width="0.949em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0.167em">mod</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)\!\!\!\!\!\!\pmod{m},\quad x_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{m}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math>, the task reduces to computing the parity of a binary sequence. From an algebraic perspective, modular addition over <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{Z}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{Z}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> (cyclic group) serves as the canonical representative for commutative operations, as every finite abelian group is isomorphic to a direct product of such cyclic groups.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We also experiment with non-commutative operations by considering the task of permutation composition over the symmetric group <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>. This task serves as the canonical non-commutative counterpart for state tracking, as by Cayley’s Theorem, every finite group is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dummit et al., 2004</a>)</cite>. For additional details and empirical results on the permutation composition task, we refer the reader to Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Permutation Composition Task ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Length Distributions:</span> 
For each generated sample, we first determine the sequence length <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\in\{2,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\in\{2,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the maximum sequence length. We then sample a sequence <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{m}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>∈</mo><msubsup><mi>ℤ</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}_{m}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without replacement</span> to ensure that every sample in the dataset is unique. We use three distinct strategies for length selection:</p>
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fixed:</span> The length is held constant at <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n=L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n=L</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Uniform:</span> Lengths are sampled uniformly at random from the set <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{2,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{2,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Short-to-Long:</span> Sequences are sampled in ascending order of length, exhausting the available sequences for length <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> before proceeding to <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n+1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n+1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task Formats:</span> We consider three task formats that vary in the density and structure of the supervision signal. Let <math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{k}=(\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i})\!\pmod{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo lspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mpadded style="width:0.219em;" width="0.219em"><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mpadded></mrow><mspace style="width:0.949em;" width="0.949em"></mspace><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">mod</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{k}=(\sum_{i=1}^{k}x_{i})\!\pmod{m}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the <math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>-th partial sum of the input sequence. The formats, illustrated in <a href="#S2.F1" title="In 2 Methodology ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, are defined as follows:</p>
<ol id="S2.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Outcome Supervision:</span> The model is provided the input sequence <math id="S2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}</annotation></semantics></math> and is trained to predict only the final sum <math id="S2.I2.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This format provides no intermediate supervision, requiring the model to discover the latent computational logic of the task on its own during training.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Chain-of-Thought (CoT):</span> The model is trained to generate the sequence of intermediate partial sums <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> following the input sequence. This decomposes the task into a sequence of iterative applications of the operator.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Aligned Chain-of-Thought (ACoT):</span> The model is tasked to output, for each input token <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, the corresponding partial sum <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. While conceptually similar to the scratchpad, this format provides per-token supervision that is aligned with the input.
This format is similarly used in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and is also referred to as <span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">state-supervision</span>.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike outcome supervision, both CoT and ACoT constitute a form of <span id="S2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">process supervision</span>, as they provide explicit training signals for the intermediate solution steps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/formats.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/92;" width="452" height="92"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Example of the three task formats for the addition modulo <math id="S2.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> task applied to the sequence <math id="S2.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2\,1\,0\,3\,4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2 1 0 3 4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\,1\,0\,3\,4</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sample Efficiency:</span> 
To quantify the data efficiency of a model under a specific task configuration, we define the <span id="S2.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">minimal sample size</span> <math id="S2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> required to learn the task reliably. Let <math id="S2.p6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> denote a training set of cardinality <math id="S2.p6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, and let <math id="S2.p6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})</annotation></semantics></math> denote the validation loss of a model trained on <math id="S2.p6.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{N}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{N}</annotation></semantics></math> using hyperparameter configuration <math id="S2.p6.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\phi\in\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\phi\in\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p7.1" class="ltx_p">We consider a task successfully learned if the minimum validation loss over the hyperparameter grid falls below a convergence threshold:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{\phi\in\Phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})\leq\epsilon," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{\phi\in\Phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})\leq\epsilon,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p7.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math> is a predefined grid of learning rates and random seeds, and <math id="S2.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> is a convergence threshold. Formally, we define <math id="S2.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> as the smallest training set size satisfying this criterion:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}=\min\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\min_{\phi\in\Phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})\leq\epsilon\right\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℕ</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>val</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϕ</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mi>ϵ</mi></mrow><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}=\min\left\{N\in\mathbb{N}:\min_{\phi\in\Phi}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\phi;\mathcal{D}_{N})\leq\epsilon\right\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p7.3" class="ltx_p">In practice, we estimate <math id="S2.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> by performing a binary search over the training set size. Note that both training and validation samples are drawn from the same underlying data generation process, and therefore <math id="S2.p7.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> reflects the <span id="S2.p7.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">in-distribution</span> sample efficiency.
In addition to low validation loss, we also consider perfect validation accuracy as an alternative success criterion and find no meaningful difference in the results. For the results in <a href="#S4" title="4 Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we use the latter.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models:</span>
We compare multi-layer decoder-only transformer architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, with two recurrent alternatives: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997</a>)</cite> and dense state-space models (Dense-SSMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fan et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Terzić et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi and Memisevic, 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In Dense<span id="S2.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>SSMs, the state transition matrix is dense and fully input<span id="S2.p9.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>dependent, a property shown to support effective state tracking in linear recurrent models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merrill et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We adopt the variant used by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi and Memisevic (2025)</a></cite>, in which input–state interactions are purely multiplicative with no additive terms:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}=A_{x_{t}}h_{t-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}=A_{x_{t}}h_{t-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p9.2" class="ltx_p">where the transition matrix <math id="S2.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A_{x_{t}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>A</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A_{x_{t}}</annotation></semantics></math> is given by a linear function of the input <math id="S2.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. This architecture is commonly referred to as a <span id="S2.p9.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">bilinear RNN</span>, since <math id="S2.p9.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> depends bilinearly on the input and the previous hidden state.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Experimental Setup:</span> 
We perform a large-scale systematic evaluation of data efficiency on synthetic state<span id="S2.p10.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>tracking tasks. To estimate <math id="S2.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, we use a hybrid binary–geometric search procedure (see Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ A.1 Search Procedure for Determining 𝑁^∗ ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) that evaluates candidate sample sizes over at most 20 steps, training models across a hyperparameter grid consisting of 3 learning rates and 5 random seeds (15 configurations total for each size <math id="S2.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>). A sample size is considered successful if at least one configuration achieves validation loss below <math id="S2.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Each model is trained for a fixed budget of <math id="S2.p10.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>250</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> optimization steps independent of the training set size <math id="S2.p10.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>. This amounts to over <span id="S2.p10.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">190,000 training runs</span> for the results reported in this paper, excluding development runs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p11.1" class="ltx_p">The transformer model used is based on the GPT-2 architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite> with 6 layers and a model (embedding/hidden) dimension of 256. Both the LSTM and Dense-SSM models use a single-layer recurrent cell followed by a linear classification head. We use input and hidden dimension of <math id="S2.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="768" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>768</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">768</annotation></semantics></math> for LSTM and <math id="S2.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math> for the Dense-SSM. Additionally, we experiment with a 2-layer transformer and LSTM with hidden dimension of <math id="S2.p11.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math>, with results provided in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Data Efficiency Evaluation for Smaller Models ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p12.1" class="ltx_p">We ensure that the training and validation sets are strictly disjoint. The validation set contains <math id="S2.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> samples (or at most <math id="S2.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the available data) and remains identical across different training set sizes, except for variations introduced by the random seed. In addition, we always use at most <math id="S2.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the available samples at each sequence length for validation, with the remainder reserved exclusively for training. Also, for all tasks, multi-digit integers are represented as single tokens during tokenization.
Additional implementation details are provided in <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>In-distribution Data Efficiency</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We perform the above binary search procedure to identify the minimal dataset size (<math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>) across all combinations of maximum sequence length <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\in\{5,10,20,30\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\in\{5,10,20,30\}</annotation></semantics></math> and modulus <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m\in\{2,3,5,10,15,20,50,75,100\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>75</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m\in\{2,3,5,10,15,20,50,75,100\}</annotation></semantics></math>, for each of the three task formats, length distributions, and models described earlier. The results are summarized in <a href="#S3.T1" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. For ease of comparison, we also visualize selected slices of this table in figures throughout this section. Comparable results for models of different sizes are reported in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Data Efficiency Evaluation for Smaller Models ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.
From the table we can infer the following key observations:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="56.54" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 56.54" 32.94 L 477.38 5.32 C 477.38 2.38 474.99 0 472.06 0 L 5.32 0 C 2.38 0 0 2.38 0 5.32 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F2F2F2;" fill="#F2F2F2" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 5.32 Z"></path></g><g transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.69 32.35)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_nestedsvg" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.34 L 0 19.85 C 0 22.25 1.94 24.19 4.34 fill="#333333" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 4.34 L 1.38 19.85 C 1.38 21.48 2.71 22.8 4.34 22.8 L 139.13 22.8 C 140.76 22.8 142.08 21.48 142.08 19.85 L 142.08 4.34 C 142.08 2.71 140.76 1.38 139.13 1.38 L 4.34 1.38 C 2.71 1.38 1.38 2.71 1.38 4.34 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 17.13 7.29)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.p2.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Observation 3.1</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 13.19 14.69)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.75em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="13.84" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 10.38)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S3.p2.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S3.p2.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p2.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Transformers prefer non-aligned supervision (Chain of Thought).</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We observe a clear preference of transformers for CoT over the Aligned CoT format.
For example, at <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=5</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L=20</annotation></semantics></math>, CoT requires 1.7K samples, while Aligned CoT requires 2M, an order<span id="S3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>of<span id="S3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>magnitude increase in sample complexity.
<a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> further illustrates this gap in sample requirements for the case <math id="S3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math> (parity) across the two formats.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">It has been hypothesized that by outputting intermediate steps autoregressively, the model can
attend to its own previous outputs, effectively simulating a larger depth circuit <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and the results confirm this hypothesis.
In contrast, Aligned Chain-of-Thought forces the model to compress the computation into a single
forward pass per token without the benefit of re-attending to intermediate results,
which appears less aligned with the transformer’s non-recurrent nature.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/cotssup.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/366;" width="462" height="366"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Minimal dataset size for the uniform length distribution with <math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math> (parity). RNNs favor ACoT, whereas transformers favor CoT.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.p5.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="56.54" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 56.54" 1.38 5.32 Z"></path></g><g transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.69 32.35)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_nestedsvg" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="matrix(1 0 0 1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 4.34 L 0 19.85 C 0 22.25 1.94 24.19 4.34 2.71 140.76 1.38 139.13 1.38 L 4.34 1.38 C 2.71 1.38 1.38 2.71 1.38 4.34 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 17.13 7.29)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.p5.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Observation 3.2</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 13.19 14.69)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.75em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.25em;font-size:10pt;" height="13.84" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 10.38)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S3.p5.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S3.p5.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p5.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Recurrent models prefer aligned supervision (Aligned Chain-of-Thought).</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Conversely, recurrent models (LSTMs and Dense-SSMs) demonstrate superior sample efficiency when trained with the Aligned CoT (ACoT) format, which provides supervision aligned with the evolution of the hidden state (see also <a href="#S3.F2" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, RNNs struggle with CoT, which is likely due to their recall bottleneck <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wen et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>:
a model must output the sequence of partial sums <math id="S3.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(s_{1},\dots,s_{n})</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S3.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">after</span> processing
the entire input sequence. This effectively requires it to unroll the chain of intermediate
computations from the beginning.
In fact, we note that under the CoT format, recurrent models even fail to generalize to longer sequences
despite their sequential inductive bias (see <a href="#A2.T2" title="In B.1 Evaluating Length-generalization ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> for length-generalization results).
The task thereby becomes bottlenecked by the model’s limited memory capacity rather than
its state-tracking ability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S3.p8.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="71.61" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 71.61" Z"></path></g><g transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.69 47.42)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_nestedsvg" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" fill="#333333" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 4.34 L 1.38 19.85 C 1.38 21.48 2.71 22.8 4.34 22.8 L 139.13 22.8 C 140.76 22.8 142.08 21.48 142.08 19.85 L 142.08 4.34 C 142.08 2.71 140.76 1.38 139.13 1.38 L 4.34 1.38 C 2.71 1.38 1.38 2.71 1.38 4.34 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 17.13 7.29)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S3.p8.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.39em;font-size:10pt;" height="28.9" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S3.p8.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S3.p8.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p8.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Recurrent models outperform transformers in the absence of intermediate supervision.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">In the Outcome Supervision setting, the model must implicitly infer the latent algebraic structure of the task solely from the final solution, without any guidance on the intermediate steps. This requires the model to effectively marginalize over unobserved computational paths with difficulty scaling with both the state space size <math id="S3.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and sequence length <math id="S3.p9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p10.1" class="ltx_p">We observe that recurrent models significantly outperform transformers in this regime. While transformers fail to converge for all but the most trivial configurations (very small <math id="S3.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>),
the recurrent architectures successfully learn the task for higher moduli and extended sequence lengths,
achieving convergence with orders of magnitude fewer training samples. <a href="#S3.F3" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> illustrates this behavior for the parity case (<math id="S3.p10.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/none.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/352;" width="462" height="352"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F3.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S3.F3.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<math id="S3.F3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> for the outcome supervision format with a uniform length distribution and <math id="S3.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math> (parity). In the absence of intermediate supervision, single<span id="S3.F3.6.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>layer RNNs significantly outperform the 6<span id="S3.F3.6.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>layer transformer.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>

style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.39em;font-size:10pt;" height="28.9" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S3.p11.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S3.p11.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.p11.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">With intermediate supervision, longer sequences improve the data efficiency of recurrent models but not transformers.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p12.1" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, under formats with intermediate supervision (CoT or ACoT), longer sequences should improve sample efficiency. This is because with intermediate solutions, the effective amount of supervised tokens increases linearly with sequence length.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">We validate this hypothesis in recurrent models trained with Aligned Chain-of-Thought: the fixed length distribution (comprising only longest sequences) yields the highest data efficiency, followed by uniform, and finally short-to-long.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, in the uniform setting, we find that recurrent models trained with ACoT require fewer data points as the maximum sequence length <math id="S3.p14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> increases, as expected. In contrast, transformers trained with CoT fail to leverage this additional supervision. This trend is also evident in <a href="#S3.F4" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, which compares sample complexity on the parity task.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/longseq.svg" id="S3.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/356;" width="462" height="356"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S3.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Sample complexity (log scale) for transformers trained with CoT and RNNs with ACoT on the parity task. RNNs exhibit the expected improvement in sample efficiency with increasing sequence length, while transformers fail to leverage the additional supervision.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S3.T1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S3.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F5.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 5</span>: </span><span id="S3.F5.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Sample complexity (log scale) in the Outcome Supervision format for the uniform and short-to-long length setting, with <math id="S3.F5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math> (parity).

</span></figcaption>

<div id="S3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p16.1" class="ltx_p">In the Outcome Supervision setting, we compare the data requirements under the uniform and short-to-long length distributions. Recall that these two distributions differ only in the order in which samples are presented during training. We observe that recurrent models require fewer samples in the short-to-long setting, suggesting that shorter sequences provide a stronger learning signal than longer sequences for these models. This effect is illustrated in <a href="#S3.F5" title="In 3 In-distribution Data Efficiency ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> for the case <math id="S3.p16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=2</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A key hypothesis for why recurrent networks dominate transformers with respect to data efficiency,
as shown in the previous section, is that their “induction bias” encourages step-by-step updates
to their representations of state. This, in turn, should allow the model
to share the same solution mechanisms across the whole sequence length.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we investigate the extent to which the learned mechanisms are shared across different sequence lengths.
Specifically, we examine whether the model develops length-specific heuristics, effectively “specialized circuits” for fixed-length sequences, or whether it has internalized the inherent inductive structure of the task.
The latter implies the discovery of a transition operator that can be applied iteratively.
Assessing the degree of this cross-length sharing is critical for understanding a model’s inductive capacity and to generalize to sequence lengths not encountered in the training distribution.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We quantify the cross-length mechanism sharing through the lens of sample efficiency. Intuitively, if a model utilizes a shared mechanism (e.g., a transition operator) across varying lengths, the sample cost to learn the task over a distribution of lengths should be significantly lower than the sum of costs to learn each length individually. This is due to the <span id="S4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">amortization</span> of the learning cost: the data required to learn the operation at length <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> simultaneously contributes to the model’s learning at length <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n+k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n+k</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Formally, we compare the total number of training examples required for
a model to simultaneously learn the task for all sequence
lengths <math id="S4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n\in\{2,\dots,L\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n\in\{2,\dots,L\}</annotation></semantics></math> (the joint task) against the sum of
samples required by <math id="S4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L-1</annotation></semantics></math> independent models, each optimized for a
single fixed length.
Let <math id="S4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}_{\text{joint}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mtext>joint</mtext><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}_{\text{joint}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the minimal sample size required for the
joint task, and <math id="S4.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the minimal sample size for a model trained
and evaluated exclusively on sequences of length <math id="S4.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.
We define the <span id="S4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Sharing Factor</span> <math id="S4.p4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> as:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=\frac{\sum_{n=2}^{L}N^{*}_{n}}{N^{*}_{\text{joint}}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mtext>joint</mtext><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=\frac{\sum_{n=2}^{L}N^{*}_{n}}{N^{*}_{\text{joint}}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p4.2" class="ltx_p">The value of <math id="S4.p4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> provides insight into the extent of across-length mechanism sharing:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math> indicates mechanism sharing and amortized learning. This suggests the model has internalized the inductive nature of the task, and data from one sequence length accelerates the acquisition of the task across the entire distribution.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\approx 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\approx 1</annotation></semantics></math> suggests that the model learns length-specific solutions in isolation, effectively partitioning capacity into independent circuits.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> represents a regime of destructive interference. In this case, the length-specific solutions compete for model capacity, making it more data-efficient to train separate models for each length than to optimize a single model for the joint task.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4 Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> illustrates the sample complexity to learn addition modulo <math id="S4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math>, for all sequence lengths (<math id="S4.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}_{\text{joint}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mtext>joint</mtext><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}_{\text{joint}}</annotation></semantics></math>), compared against the cumulative samples required by independent models trained on individual sequence lengths (<math id="S4.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{n=2}^{L}N^{*}_{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msubsup><mi>N</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=2}^{L}N^{*}_{n}</annotation></semantics></math>), for <math id="S4.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L\in\{2,\dots,10\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L\in\{2,\dots,10\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We evaluate these metrics for modular addition with <math id="S4.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=5</annotation></semantics></math> across the three previously defined task formats, and draw the following key observations. Comparable results for the permutation composition task (symmetric group <math id="S4.p5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>) are reported in Appendix <a href="#A2.SS2" title="B.2 Permutation Composition Task ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.p6.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="55" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 55" class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.p6.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S4.p6.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p6.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Transformers have low sharing factor for all task formats.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">As demonstrated, we observe a low sharing factor in transformers across all task formats, with <math id="S4.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\approx 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\approx 1</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math> in all cases. Notably, in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) setting, despite being transformer’s most efficient task configuration, we observe an extreme case of length isolation (<math id="S4.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa=0.28" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.28</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa=0.28</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.p8.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="52.31" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 52.31" </div>
<div id="S4.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p9.1" class="ltx_p">The observed sharing factor of <math id="S4.p9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\ll 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≪</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\ll 1</annotation></semantics></math> for transformer with CoT indicates a regime of destructive interference where length-specific solutions compete for model capacity, such that training on a diverse length distribution is substantially less data-efficient than training independent models on each length.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.p10.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="68.92" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 68.92" 1.38 5.32 Z"></path></g><g transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.69 44.73)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_nestedsvg" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000"
