2.71 140.76 1.38 139.13 1.38 L 4.34 1.38 C 2.71 1.38 1.38 2.71 1.38 4.34 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 17.13 7.29)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.p10.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Observation 4.3</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 13.19 27.83)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:1.2em;font-size:10pt;" height="26.21" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.p10.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S4.p10.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p10.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Recurrent networks have high sharing factors in their preferred task formats.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p11.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, both recurrent models exhibit clear evidence of mechanism sharing and amortized learning across sequence lengths (<math id="S4.p11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\gg 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\gg 1</annotation></semantics></math>) under the Outcome Supervision and Aligned Chain-of-Thought formats. However, this is no longer the case in the Chain-of-Thought format (<math id="S4.p11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\approx 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\approx 1</annotation></semantics></math>), where the recurrent models also fail to share across the sequence lengths, likely due to the previously discussed recall bottleneck. However, unlike transformers, we do not observe destructive interference in this case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.p12.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="55" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 55" 1.38 5.32 Z"></path></g><g transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 19.69 30.81)"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" class="ltx_nestedsvg" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" fill="#333333" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.38 4.34 L 1.38 19.85 C 1.38 21.48 2.71 22.8 4.34 22.8 L 139.13 22.8 C 140.76 22.8 142.08 21.48 142.08 19.85 L 142.08 4.34 C 142.08 2.71 140.76 1.38 139.13 1.38 L 4.34 1.38 C 2.71 1.38 1.38 2.71 1.38 4.34 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 17.13 7.29)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.p12.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">Observation 4.4</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 13.19 13.92)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.p12.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S4.p12.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p12.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Longer sequences increase data efficiency for Dense-SSMs.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p13.1" class="ltx_p">As noted in the previous section, the sample requirement for the Dense-SSM under ACoT <span id="S4.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">decreases</span> as the maximum sequence length <math id="S4.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> increases. This indicates that through cross-length mechanism sharing, the model leverages the higher density of supervision signals in longer sequences.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F6" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/circuit_ModularAddition_3.svg" id="S4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:476/384;" width="476" height="384"></object>
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S4.F6.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S4.F6.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

The results suggest that transformers learn largely isolated solutions for each sequence length.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S4.p14.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="55" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 477.38 55" style="--ltx-fo-width:6.92em;--ltx-fo-height:0.6em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:11.5pt;" height="9.61" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="110.09"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="S4.p14.pic1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fo-width:32.59em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="450.95"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S4.p14.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:32.59em;">
<span id="S4.p14.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.p14.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">OOD generalization implies high sharing factor, and vice versa.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
<div id="S4.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p15.1" class="ltx_p">Interestingly, we observe a consistent correlation between the sharing factor <math id="S4.p15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>κ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa</annotation></semantics></math> and length generalization:
cases with high sharing factor (<math id="S4.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\gg 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≫</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\gg 1</annotation></semantics></math>) correspond to those in which the model learns
a length-generalizable solution (see <a href="#A2.T2" title="In B.1 Evaluating Length-generalization ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
Conversely, cases with low sharing factor (<math id="S4.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\kappa\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>κ</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\kappa\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>) are precisely those in which the learned
solution fails to extrapolate beyond the training sequence lengths.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p16.1" class="ltx_p">This provides additional evidence that in-distribution data efficiency and circuit sharing are fundamental implications
of length generalization in state tracking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our study indicates that state tracking poses severe challenges for
transformer-based sequence models not only out-of-distribution but also
in-distribution:
They require extraordinarily large amounts of training data to
generalize on simple tasks and require Chain-of-Thought supervision
to learn in-distribution on even moderate sequence lengths.
This suggests that end-to-end learning in applied “agentic” scenarios,
such as robotics or GUI control, could be even more challenging.
The fact that data requirements scale with sequence length may
also help explain well-known challenges at large context
lengths (“context rot”).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We study performance across a limited, albeit representative, number of models and task types.
Unfortunately, the large search space over parameters (performed using binary search in our experiments) requires a number of many thousand
individual training runs.
This makes this comparison highly computationally demanding even for the current set of models
and tasks. However, as models were chosen to be simple and representative it seems very likely
that the findings will persist even under slight model variations, similar to how they did
in previous OOD studies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine
Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none
which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Search Procedure for Determining <math id="A1.SS1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math></h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To identify the minimal sample size <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N^{*}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>N</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> required for a model to successfully learn a target task, we use a hybrid Binary-Geometric search as described in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ A.1 Search Procedure for Determining 𝑁^∗ ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The algorithm conducts a search over sample sizes, combining an initial exponential reduction phase with a subsequent binary search phase.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The search begins at a predefined maximum sample size <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{max}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>max</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{max}}</annotation></semantics></math>. For any candidate size <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>, the algorithm trains models using multiple configurations drawn from a fixed hyperparameter grid <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Phi" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi</annotation></semantics></math>. In our implementation, each evaluation consists of 15 model instances (3 learning rates <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> 5 random seeds). A sample size <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is considered successful if at least one configuration attains validation loss below a threshold <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, in which case we decrease the next sample size, and otherwise, the size is labeled unsuccessful and the next trial size is increased.</p>
</div>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="A1.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We use a geometric multiplier of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=1000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=1000</annotation></semantics></math>, a maximum of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S=20</annotation></semantics></math> search steps, and a success threshold of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>. The hyperparameter grid is</p>
<table id="A1.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Phi=\{\text{LR}\in\{10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5}\}\}\times\{\text{seed}\in\{10,20,30,40,50\}\}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Φ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>LR</mtext><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mtext>seed</mtext><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Phi=\{\text{LR}\in\{10^{-3},10^{-4},10^{-5}\}\}\times\{\text{seed}\in\{10,20,30,40,50\}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">yielding 15 configurations per evaluation. Each model is trained for a fixed budget of <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="250\text{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>250</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>k</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">250\text{k}</annotation></semantics></math> optimization steps with batch size <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="64" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>64</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">64</annotation></semantics></math> using the Adam optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2014</a>)</cite>, independent of the training set size <math id="A1.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math>. This implies a maximum feasible sample size of</p>
<table id="A1.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\max}=250{,}000\times 64=16\text{M}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>250,000</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>M</mtext></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\max}=250{,}000\times 64=16\text{M}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The maximum training set size is the minimum between the feasible <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="16\text{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>M</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">16\text{M}</annotation></semantics></math> samples and the total number of sequences available under the specified configuration of maximum sequence length <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> and modulus <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m^{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>L</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m^{L}</annotation></semantics></math> for the <span id="A1.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Fixed</span> distribution, and <math id="A1.SS1.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{n=1}^{L}m^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>L</mi></msubsup><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{n=1}^{L}m^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> for the uniform and short-to-long distributions (see <a href="#S2" title="2 Methodology ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>). The final training set size is obtained after deducting the validation set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Evaluation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We ensure that the training and validation sets are strictly disjoint. The validation set contains <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}000</annotation></semantics></math> samples (or at most <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the available data) and remains identical across different training set sizes, except for variations introduced by the random seed. In addition, we always use at most <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="20\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">20\%</annotation></semantics></math> of the available samples at each sequence length for validation, with the remainder reserved exclusively for training. Also, for all tasks, multi-digit integers are represented as single tokens during tokenization. Finally, for the Chain-of-Thought task format, validation loss is computed using teacher forcing rather than autoregressive sampling.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Models</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The transformer model is based on the GPT-2 architecture <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, with <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="6" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>6</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">6</annotation></semantics></math> layers and a model (embedding/hidden) dimension of 256. Other architectural parameters, including an MLP expansion factor of <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>4</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">4</annotation></semantics></math>, follow the default GPT-2 (small) settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Both the LSTM and Dense-SSM use a single-layer recurrent cell followed by a linear classification head to map the hidden state to token logits. We use an input and hidden dimension of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="768" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>768</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">768</annotation></semantics></math> for the LSTM, and <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math> for the Dense-SSM. See <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ebrahimi and Memisevic (2025)</a></cite> for additional details on the Bilinear architecture used for Dense-SSM. We also experiment with a <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2</annotation></semantics></math>-layer transformer and a single-layer LSTM with a hidden dimensionality of <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="256" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>256</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">256</annotation></semantics></math>; sample-efficiency results for these variants are provided in the Appendix <a href="#A2.SS3" title="B.3 Data Efficiency Evaluation for Smaller Models ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional Experimental Results</h2>

<section id="A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>Permutation Composition Task</h3>

<div id="A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Task:</span> 
To show our findings generalize beyond commutative operations, we consider the task of permutation composition (simulating the symmetric group <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>). Each element of the group represents a permutation of the set <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{1,\dots,m\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{1,\dots,m\}</annotation></semantics></math>, resulting in a group of cardinality <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|S_{m}|=m!" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|S_{m}|=m!</annotation></semantics></math>. In our experimental setup, each permutation <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi\in S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi\in S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is bijectively mapped to a unique integer token in <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{0,1,\dots,m!-1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{0,1,\dots,m!-1\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given an input sequence of <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> permutations <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots,\pi_{n})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}=(\pi_{1},\pi_{2},\dots,\pi_{n})</annotation></semantics></math>, the model is required to compute their sequential composition:</p>
<table id="A2.E5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y=\pi_{n}\circ\pi_{n-1}\circ\dots\circ\pi_{1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">⋯</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">∘</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y=\pi_{n}\circ\pi_{n-1}\circ\dots\circ\pi_{1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\circ" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∘</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\circ</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the permutation composition operator. This task significantly elevates the complexity of state tracking, as the model can no longer rely on the order-invariance property characteristic of abelian groups.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algebraic Significance:</span> 
The symmetric group <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the canonical non-commutative structure for evaluating state tracking. Its fundamental importance is grounded in <span id="A2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Cayley’s Theorem</span>, which states that every finite group <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>G</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G</annotation></semantics></math> is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{|G|}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>G</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{|G|}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dummit et al., 2004</a>)</cite>. Hence, by analyzing performance on <math id="A2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, we effectively probe the model’s capacity to internalize the transition dynamics of any finite discrete group.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As noted in <a href="#A2.F7" title="In B.2 Permutation Composition Task ‣ Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we observe the same patterns described in <a href="#S4" title="4 Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Section</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4 Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, supporting the generalization of these findings and the subsequent arguments to non<span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">-</span>commutative state<span id="A2.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">-</span>tracking tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A2.F7" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18333v1/circuit_SymmetricGroup_3.svg" id="A2.SS2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:457/369;" width="457" height="369"></object>
<br class="ltx_break ltx_break">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A2.F7.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 7</span>: </span><span id="A2.F7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
Similar to <a href="#S4.F6" title="In 4 Weight Sharing Across Sequence Length ‣ On the “Induction Bias” in Sequence Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, but for permutation composition task (<math id="A2.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>). The results suggest that transformers learn largely isolated solutions for each sequence length.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
